topic: Both too little and too much sleep are linked to earlier death
subject: health

facts.claim: No significant difference was identified for periods of self-reported sleep <7 hours.
facts.quote: No significant difference was identified for periods of self-reported sleep <7 hours, whereas similar patterns were observed for stroke and cardiovascular disease mortality.

facts.claim: The overall risk difference for all-cause mortality was 0.09 (95% CI 0.07-0.11) favouring the >9 h group compared with the 7-9 h group.
facts.quote: The overall RD for all-cause mortality was 0. 09 (95% CI 0. 07-0. 11) favouring the >9 h group compared with our reference.

facts.claim: The risk of death for 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10 and 11 hours/day of nighttime sleep was 1.09, 1.21, 1.37, 1.55, 1.37, 1.55, and 1.84 respectively.
facts.quote: 09), 1. 21 (1. 18-1. 24), 1. 37 (1. 32-1. 42) and 1. 55 (1. 47-1. 63) for 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10 and 11 hours/day of nighttime sleep, respectively

facts.claim: Long duration of sleep is linked to a 1.30 risk of death (1.22 to 1.38; P < 0.0001).
facts.quote: Long duration of sleep was also associated with a greater risk of death (1. 30; [1. 22 to 1. 38]; P < 0. 0001)

facts.claim: For all-cause mortality, when sleep duration was 7 hours per day, the pooled RR was 1.13 (95% CI, 1.11-1.15) per 1-hour increment.
facts.quote: For all-cause mortality, when sleep duration was 7 hours per day, the pooled RR was 1. 13 (95% CI, 1. 11-1. 15) per 1-hour increment.
facts.causalWarning: causal wording, but the cited study only shows an association

facts.claim: Short duration of sleep is linked to a 1.12 risk of death (95% CI 1.06 to 1.18; P < 0.01).
facts.quote: In the pooled analysis, short duration of sleep was associated with a greater risk of death (RR: 1. 12; 95% CI 1. 06 to 1. 18; P < 0. 01)

research.angle: While some studies show both short and long sleep are linked to higher mortality, other evidence suggests that only long sleep duration is significantly linked to increased risk.
research.verdict: The evidence shows a general trend that both extremes of sleep duration are linked to adverse health outcomes, but the strength and significance of the risk for short sleep vary significantly across different meta-analyses.
research.caveat: Some findings regarding long sleep may reflect underlying systemic or neurological diseases that cause sleep fragmentation rather than the duration itself.
